1957 Pontiac Chieftain Sat in a Barn for 54 Years, Unrestored Survivor
7 photos
Photo: Bob Boecker/Facebook Marketplace
1957 was a great year for American-made cars. Ford introduced the Ranchero and Fairlane 500 Skyliner, and Mercury debuted the Turnpike Cruiser , while Pontiac launched the Bonneville. The Rambler Rebel also arrived that year as one of America's first muscle cars. Chevrolet restyled the Tri-Five lineup, creating the most iconic iteration of the Bel Air and Nomad.
Picking a favorite from this model year is pretty much mission impossible for me. All these cars have quite a few achievements to brag about. I'm most tempted to go with the Turnpike Cruiser here, but the Bonneville would be a close second. By the way, the latter wasn't yet a stand-alone model but a luxurious, high-performance convertible based on the Star Chief.
But the Chevy Bel Air is by far the most iconic classic from this list. 1957 the third and final year for the Tri-Five version, which has now morphed into a very desirable vehicle, especially in two-door hardtop trim. But while I also like the Bel Air, I always felt that the contemporary Pontiac Chieftain was a cooler option.
How so? Well, for starters, I'm a big 1950s Poncho guy. But I also think that Pontiac's A-body cars look much better. There's something cool about those massive bumpers, more prominent headlamps, and stylish, rocket-inspired taillights. Which brings me to this 1957 two-door that emerged from a barn after over 50 decades.
Hailing from Chanhassen, Minnesota, this Chieftain was reportedly parked in 1972. This means that it spent a whopping 54 years in a barn. But despite being off the road for so long, it's still in pretty good condition. Apparently barn conditions weren't all that bad in this case (which is mighty rare).
The vehicle is described as unrestored, and the photos confirm this scenario. However, it's not a fully fledged survivor. One of the front fenders is finished in a different color, which suggests that the original item may have been replaced before the car went into storage. This Chieftain may have been involved in an accident, but there's no word on that in the ad.
The only photo of the interior shows a two-tone, gray-and-white cabin that's still sound. The upholstery is weathered, and there are cracks in the steering wheel, but it's complete and appears to be all-original .
There are no photos of the engine bay, but the seller mentions a 347-cubic-inch (5.7-liter) V8 mill. The displacement is correct for the 1957 Chieftain, which received a larger powerplant that year. The 347 V8 replaced the previous 317-cubic-inch (5.2-liter) V8.
The unit was available in various forms, starting with a base two-barrel configuration rated at 227 horsepower. A higher-compression version delivered 252 horsepower, while the optional Tri-Power unit came with up to 317 horsepower on tap. There's no word on which version this Chieftain has, but the ad mentions that the motor turns over. That's great news after 54 years without a sip of gasoline.
The two-door coupe is available for $3,250 , which isn't bad for a 1957 Poncho in this condition. Is this Chieftain worth restoring? Let me know in the comments section below.
